region.en: Forest south of the Silla palace (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅宮南林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Silla annal legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 66

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 8, eBook #52127

summary.en: The king of Silla is wakened by loud cackling of a hen from the forest to the south. A messenger finds a box hanging from a branch with a white hen cluttering on the ground beneath; opening it, the king discovers a handsome child named Keum Yun-ji. Up to this time the kingdom had been called Su-ra-bul, but now the king renames it Kye-rim — kye meaning hen and rim woods — the Hen in the Woods, not a very dignified name but one that fitted the kingdom.
summary.zh: 新羅王夜聞林中雞鳴，遣人探之，見樹上有櫝，下有白雞伏於地。啟櫝得一俊兒，名金閼智。國名本為徐羅伐，至是改稱雞林——雞者雞也，林者林也。

sensitivity.note: Silla annal legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The year 66 brought forth another of those wonders that embellish the legendary lore of Korea. The king of Sil-la was wakened one night by the loud cackling of a hen, which seemed to come from a forest to the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 8 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A messenger was sent to see what was the cause of the disturbance, and he found a box hanging from the branch of a tree, while on the ground beneath it there cluttered a white hen. When the box was placed before the king and he had opened it, a handsome child was found. It received the name Keum Yun-ji.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 8 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some say this Yun-ji was merely a part of the name, while others affirm that it is a pure Sil-la word meaning baby. Up to this time the kingdom had been called Su-ra-bul, but now the king changed it to Kye-rim, kye meaning hen and rim woods, so the kingdom was called the Hen in the Woods — not a very dignified name, but one, perhaps, that fitted well the military prowess of the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 8 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Yung-o and Se-o Carried to Japan on the Rock

region.zh: 新羅東海岸（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Silla annal legend, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 158

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 8, eBook #52127

summary.en: The poor fisherman Yung-o is seated on a great boulder beside the Japan Sea when the rock trembles and rises straight into the air, carrying him east across the sea to a Japanese village, where the people take him for a god and make him their king. His wife Se-o mounts the same rock to search for him and is carried the same way; she finds him transformed into a king and becomes his queen. But their departure darkens Silla: sun and moon fail, the land is shrouded in gloom, and the soothsayers say someone has gone to Japan. Only when Se-o sends a roll of silk, and the Silla king spreads it out and sacrifices upon it with words of invocation, does the sunlight burst forth again.
summary.zh: 漁父甕顧坐海邊巨石垂釣，石忽震動凌空，載之東渡，落於倭國村中。倭人以為神，立為王。其妻細烏尋夫，登同一之石，亦被載往，見夫已為王，遂為王后。然二人去國而新羅日月失明，天地晦冥；卜者云有人東渡故也。使者往請，夫妻不歸，細烏乃付綾羅一匹，囑國王展布其上而祭之；王如其言誦咒，日光頓復，天下泰然。

sensitivity.note: Sun-restoration ritual legend; parallels the sun-capture cluster (Maui-type) across traditions.

passages.text: The interesting legend of Yung-o and Se-o belongs to the year 158. Yung-o, a poor fisherman, lived with his wife Se-o beside the waters of the Japan Sea on the eastern shore of Sil-la. One day as Yung-o was seated on a great boulder beside the water, fishing, he felt the rock tremble and then rise straight in air. He was carried, to his great consternation, eastward across the sea and deposited in a Japanese village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 8 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Japanese folk took him for a god and made him their king at once. When his wife found that he did not return from fishing she went in search of him. Ascending the same rock that had carried him to Japan she experienced the same novel extradition; she found him metamorphosed into a king and was nothing loath to become queen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 8 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: But their departure brought disaster to Sil-la, for the sun and moon were darkened and the land was shrouded in gloom. The sooth-sayers said it was because someone had gone to Japan. An envoy was sent post haste to those islands in search of the fugitives, but found to his dismay that they had become king and queen of one of the kingdoms there. He told his story and besought them to return, but they seemed well satisfied with the change.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 8 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Se-o, however, brought out a roll of silk and gave it to the envoy, saying that if the king of Sil-la would spread it out and sacrifice upon it, the light would return. The event proved the truth of her statement; and when the king uttered the words of invocation the sunlight burst forth again and all was well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 8 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Three Sages and the Floating Chests of Cheju

region.zh: 濟州三姓穴（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tamna founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated the dawn of history

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 10, eBook #52127

summary.en: Tradition says that when the island of Che-ju was covered only with tangled forest, three sages arose from a crevice in the ground — the spot is shown to this day. Standing on the shore they saw three stout chests floating in from the south-east; opening them they found in each a calf, a colt, a dog, a pig and a woman, together with seeds of beans, wheat, barley, millet and rice. By the three families thus organised the island was populated.
summary.zh: 相傳太古濟州荊榛未闢，有神人三人自地穴中出（穴至今猶存）。立於海濱，見三櫝自東南浮來，負之登岸而啟之：每櫝中有牛犢、馬駒、犬、豕與一婦人，並豆、麥、大麥、黍、稻五穀之種。三族既立，島中遂有人煙。

sensitivity.note: Cheju (Tamna) founding tradition still venerated at the Samseonghyeol shrine; recorded here as annalistic tradition, not living liturgy.

passages.text: Tradition says that in the dawn of history, when the island of Che-ju was covered only with a tangled forest, three sages arose from a crevice in the ground. This spot is shown to this day by the people of Che-ju. These three men were Ko-ulla, Yang-ulla and Pu-ulla.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they stood upon the shore they saw three stout chests floating in from the south-east. Drawing them to land and opening them, the three wise men discovered that each chest contained a calf, a colt, a dog, a pig and a woman, together with sundry seeds, such as beans, wheat, barley, millet and rice. By the three families thus organised the island was populated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Friend Star and the Naming of Tamna

texts.period: Tamna founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated early Silla

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 10, eBook #52127

summary.en: During the early days of Silla a court astrologer announces that the Friend Star is visible in the south and that a distinguished visitor will soon arrive. Soon three men come by boat from Quelpart and land at T'am-jin harbor. The king names the first Sung-ju, Lord of the Star, the second Wang-ja, King's Son, and the third Tona, The One who has Come; he names their country T'am after the port and na for kingdom, the same root that ends Sil-la — the root of the modern Korean word nara, kingdom.
summary.zh: 新羅初，太史奏南方客星現，將有大賓至。未幾，濟州三人浮舟來朝，泊於耽津。王賜名曰星主、王子、徒內，並以其國名耽羅——耽取泊地之名，羅即國也，與新羅之羅同根，即今語云拿剌（國）者是。

sensitivity.note: Tamna naming legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: During the early days of Sil-la a certain court astrologer announced that the Friend Star was visible in the south and that a distinguished visitor would soon arrive. Soon after this three men came by boat from Quelpart, landing at the harbor of T'am-jin, now Kang-jin. They came straight to the court of Sil-la where they were hospitably entertained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the visitors was Ko-hu, one was Ko-ch'ung, but the name of the third is lost. The king called the first Sung-ju, Lord of the Star; the second Wang-ja, King's Son; and the third Tona, The One who has Come. He named their country T'am from the name of the port where they landed, and na, which seems to have meant kingdom, for we find that the last syllable of Sil-la is this same na changed by euphonic laws to la. So the kingdom was called T'am-na.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Ichadon's Blood Runs White as Milk

texts.period: Silla hagiographic legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 527 (Hulbert dates the execution 524)

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 10, eBook #52127

summary.en: The courtiers of Silla, alarmed that the king has fallen wholly under the monks' influence, press him to execute the high priest Yi Cha-don (Ichadon). Tradition says that at the scaffold he exclaimed: when you slay me, my blood will flow not red like blood but white as milk, and then you will know that Buddhism is true. And so it proved: when his head was severed, his blood flowed white as milk. None could gainsay the evidence, and from that day Buddhism advanced with rapid steps; the following year the king made a law against the killing of animals.
summary.zh: 新羅群臣懼僧勢之盛，迫王誅高僧異次頓。刑前異次頓宣言：『若斬我頭，血當不赤而白如乳，爾曹可知佛法不虛。』及刑，血果白如乳。舉國無敢異言，自是佛法大行。翌年王遂下令禁殺生。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist martyr miracle central to Silla history; no living-community restriction on retelling.

passages.text: The king had come so completely under the influence of the monks that now in 524 the courtiers feared that their power would be seriously threatened. They therefore used every means to induce the king to moderate his views. The king gave his reluctant assent to the execution of the high priest, Yi Cha-don.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tradition says that when he was brought to execution he exclaimed, 'When you slay me, my blood will flow not red like blood but white as milk, and then you will know that Buddhism is true.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: And so it proved, for when his head was severed from the trunk his blood flowed white like milk. None could gainsay this evidence, and from that day Buddhism advanced with rapid steps. The following year the king made a law against the killing of animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.

texts.period: Silla decline omens from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); events scattered over the eighth and ninth centuries AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 13, eBook #52127

summary.en: As Silla declines, tradition preserves a catalogue of portents prophetic of the fall: a white rainbow pierces the sun, the sea turns to blood, hail falls like hens' eggs, a monastery is shaken sixteen times, a cow brings forth five calves at a birth, two suns rise together, three stars fall and fight in the palace, the land subsides fifty feet and fills with blue-black water, a tiger enters the palace, boulders rise and stand alone and move a hundred paces by themselves, pagodas fight each other, snow falls in September, and a whirlwind starts from the grave of Kim Yu-sin and stops at the grave of Hyokkose — all pointing toward the coming catastrophe.
summary.zh: 新羅之衰，史載妖異屢見以為亡徵：白虹貫日、海血如潮、雹大如雞卵、寺震十六、一產五犢、二日並出、三星隕而鬥於宮、地陷五十尺而水青黑、虎入宮闕、黑霧蔽野、巨石自立而獨行百步、雙塔相擊、九月降雪、杏再花，尤奇者，旋風自金庾信墓起而止於赫居世王陵。韓人皆以為覆亡之兆。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic omen catalogue; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The story of the next century and a half is the story of Sil-la's decline and fall. The following is the list of omens which tradition cites as being prophetic of that event: a white rainbow pierced the sun; the sea turned to blood; hail fell of the size of hens' eggs; a monastery was shaken sixteen times by an earthquake; a cow brought forth five calves at a time; two suns arose together; three stars fell and fought together in the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 13 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A tract of land subsided fifty feet and the hollow filled with blue black water; a tiger came into the palace; a black fog covered the land; famines and plagues were common; a hurricane blew over two of the palace gates; a huge boulder rose on end and stood by itself; two pagodas at a monastery fought with each other; snow fell in September; at Han-yang a boulder moved a hundred paces all by itself; stones fought with each other; a shower of worms fell; apricot trees bloomed twice in a year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 13 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A whirlwind started from the grave of Kim Yu-sin and stopped at the grave of Hyuk-ku-se. These omens were scattered through a series of years, but to the Korean they all point toward the coming catastrophe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 13 (1905); not verbatim.

texts.period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 878

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Kung-ye, son of King Hon-gang by a concubine, is born on the least auspicious day of the year, the fifth of the fifth moon, and with teeth already in his mouth. The king orders the child destroyed, so he is thrown out of the window — but the nurse rescues him, and in carrying him to safety accidentally puts out one of his eyes. He grows to manhood, becomes a monk under the name Sun-jong, then joins bandit camps and rises to found his own kingdom.
summary.zh: 弓裔者，新羅憲康王庶子也。生於五月五日大凶之日，口已有齒，王命棄之，遂擲於窗下。乳母竊而育之，途中誤傷其一目。長為僧，號善宗，後投賊中，終自建國號泰封。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic biographical legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Kung-ye was the son of King Hon-gang by a concubine. He was born on the least auspicious day of the year, the fifth of the fifth moon. He had several teeth when he was born, which made his arrival the less welcome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King ordered the child to be destroyed, so it was thrown out of the window. But the nurse rescued it and carried it to a place of safety where she nursed it and provided for its bringing up. As she was carrying the child she accidentally put out one of its eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he reached man's estate he became a monk under the name of Sun-jong. He was by nature ill fitted for the monastic life, and soon found himself in the camp of the bandit Ki-whun at Chuk-ju, where his talents were better appreciated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mock Buddha Who Read Minds

texts.period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 911-918

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Kung-ye proclaims himself a Buddha called Mi-ryuk-pul, dresses as a high priest and goes nowhere without censers. Heated to madness, he thrusts a white-hot iron bar into his wife's womb and kills his sons. When he suddenly orders the popular young general Wang-gon to the capital and accuses him of conspiracy — claiming to read men's minds through his sacred office — a clerk drops his pen beside the prostrate Wang-gon and whispers: confess that you have conspired. Wang-gon confesses; the mock Buddha is delighted at his own supposed power of reading minds, forgives him, and seals his own doom.
summary.zh: 弓裔僭號彌勒佛，衣袈裟，持香爐，自謂能讀人心。狂疾日深，烙妻殺子。一日忽召大將王建至京，誣以謀逆，曰『俟吾內證』。俯首良久，有書吏故墮筆於地，俯拾而竊語王建：『自承之！』王建悟，遂自認。偽佛大喜，自謂真有他心通，厚賜而縱之，實自速其亡。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic biographical legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In 911 Kung-ye changed the name of his kingdom to Taebong. It is probable that this was because of a strong Buddhistic tendency that had at this time quite absorbed him. He proclaimed himself a Buddha, called himself Mi-ryuk-pul, dressed as a high priest and went nowhere without censers. He pretended to teach the tenets of Buddhism.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Kung-ye became so infatuated that he seemed little better than a madman. He heated an iron to a white heat and thrust it into his wife's womb because she continually tried to dissuade him from his Buddhistic notions. He followed this up by killing both his sons, and was hated as thoroughly as he was feared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddenly Kung-ye ordered the young general Wang-gon up to the capital and exclaimed, 'You conspired against me yesterday.' The young man calmly asked how. Kung-ye pretended to know it through the power of his sacred office as Buddha, and said, 'Wait, I will again consult the inner consciousness.' Bowing his head he pretended to commune with his inner self.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this moment one of the clerks purposely dropped his pen, letting it roll near the prostrate form of Wang-gon. As the clerk stooped to pick it up he whispered, 'Confess that you have conspired.' When the mock Buddha raised his head and repeated the accusation, Wang-gon confessed that it was true. The King was delighted, believing he had actually acquired the faculty of reading men's minds, readily forgave the offence and gave Wang-gon rich gifts — and in this blind confidence sealed his own fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mirror with the Riddle of Two Kings

region.zh: 鐵原泰封宮（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. AD 918

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: A Chinese merchant buys a mirror of a Silla man, and in the mirror these words can be seen: Between three waters — God sends his son to Chin and Ma — First seize a hen and then a duck — in the year Ki-ja two dragons will arise, one in a green forest and one east of black metal. The merchant presents it to Kung-ye, who prizes it and seeks everywhere for the solution, until the scholar Song Han-hong explains: Chin-han and Ma-han are the two Hans; the hen is Kye-rim (Silla); the duck is the duck-blue Amnok River; the green forest is pine, Song-do, the Pine Tree Capital; and black metal is Ch'ul-wun. So a king must arise in Song-do, Wang-gon, and a king must fall in Ch'ul-wun, Kung-ye.
summary.zh: 唐商買新羅人古鏡，背有讖曰：『三水之間，上帝遣子於辰韓馬韓；先取雞，後取鴨；甲子年二龍起，一在青林，一在玄金之東。』弓裔寶之，遍求解者。學士宋含弘解曰：雞者雞林（新羅），鴨者鴨綠江，青林者松岳松京（王建興處），玄金者鐵原（弓裔亡處）。故松京當出王，鐵原當出亡。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic prophecy legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tradition says that the fall of Kung-ye was all in fulfillment of a prophecy given in the form of an enigma. A Chinese merchant bought a mirror of a Sil-la man, and in the mirror could be seen these words: 'Between three waters — God sends his son to Chin and Ma — First seize a hen and then a duck — in the year Ki-ja two dragons will arise, one in a green forest and one east of black metal.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The merchant presented it to Kung-ye, who prized it highly and sought everywhere for the solution of the riddle. At last the scholar Song Han-hong solved it: the Chin and Ma mean Chin-han and Ma-han; the hen is Kye-rim, Silla; the duck is the Am-nok, the duck-blue River; the green forest is pine tree, or Song-do, the Pine Tree Capital; and black metal is Ch'ul-wun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: So a king in Song-do must arise, Wang-gon, and a king in Ch'ul-wun must fall, Kung-ye.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monk Toson Foretells a Great Man

region.zh: 松岳王龍家（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated before AD 878

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: The birth of Wang-gon, founder of Koryo, had long been prophesied by the monk Toson, who told Wang-yong as he was building his house that a great man would be born within its walls, and left with him a letter to be given to the unborn child when he could read. When the boy was seventeen the same monk reappeared, became his tutor, instructed him in the art of war, and showed him how to obtain aid from the heavenly powers and to sacrifice to the spirits of mountain and stream so as to propitiate them. The night the boy was born, a luminous cloud stood above the house and made it as bright as day.
summary.zh: 高麗太祖王建之生，僧道詵早有預言。當王隆宅第將成，道詵語之曰：『此屋內當生大人物。』臨去，遺書一封，囑俟其子長成授之。建生之夜，家有光雲，燭室如晝。及年十七，道詵復至，為其師，授兵法，並教以祈天助、祭山川之神之法。

sensitivity.note: Koryo dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Sil-la, AD 878: the night the boy was born a luminous cloud stood above the house and made it as bright as day, so the story runs. The child had a very high forehead and a square chin, and he developed rapidly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: His birth had long since been prophesied by a monk named To-sun, who told Wang-yung, as he was building his house, that within its walls a great man would be born. As the monk turned to go, Wang-yung called him back and received from him a letter which he was ordered to give to the yet unborn child when he should be old enough to read.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the boy reached his seventeenth year the same monk reappeared and became his tutor, instructing him especially in the art of war. He showed him also how to obtain aid from the heavenly powers, and how to sacrifice to the spirits of mountain and stream so as to propitiate them. Such is the tradition that surrounds the origin of the youth who, in the troubled days of Sil-la, founded the kingdom of Koryo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Priest of the Hand-Washing Water

texts.period: Koryo annal anecdote, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 1182

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: In the twelfth year of the reign, 1182, a priest claims to be able to cure any disease. Called before the king, he explains: if anyone drinks water in which I have washed my hands he will be immediately cured; after drinking, pray earnestly to Buddha, rise and say 'I am cured', and if you really believe you are cured, you will be so. Crowds of people apply for treatment — and he seduces many of the women who come to him.
summary.zh: 高麗明宗十二年（1182），有僧自言能治百病。王召問之，對曰：『凡飲我洗手之水，其病立愈。飲後當至誠念佛，起而自呼「我愈矣」，誠信則必效。』求療者雲集，僧乘機污其婦女。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic anecdote about fraudulent healing; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the twelfth year of the reign, 1182, we find an interesting application of what goes in these days under the name of faith cure. A priest claimed to be able to cure any disease.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Being called before the king he said, 'If anyone drinks water in which I have washed my hands he will be immediately cured.' He further explained, 'After drinking the water, pray earnestly to Buddha. Then rise and say I am cured; and if you really believe you are cured, you will be so.'

title.en: The Tana Well Filled with Earth

region.zh: 太男井，松京（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Koryo annal anecdote, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. AD 1196

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: A saying current among the people shows how superstitious they were and how the eunuchs abused their power: if the King uses water from the Ta-na Wall, many eunuchs will arise and cause the government to be administered badly. So the well was filled up.
summary.zh: 松京有諺曰：『王飲太男井水，則閹宦必盛而政亂。』遂填其井以絕之。

passages.text: There was a saying current among the people which shows at once how superstitious they were and to what an extent the eunuchs were wont to abuse their power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They said, 'If the King uses water from the Ta-na Wall, many eunuchs will arise and will cause the government to be administered badly'; so the well was filled up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Plum Trees Mutilated for the Yi

region.zh: 雞龍山，忠清道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Choson founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1392-1394

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: With the beginning of the new dynasty a new capital must be founded, and King Tae-jo first begins work at Kyeryong Mountain. But it is found that in Silla days the celebrated priest Toson prophesied that in days to come Yi would found a capital at Han-yang, and one of the Koryu kings, planting many plum trees there, had them mutilated as fast as they matured, hoping thus to harm the fortunes of the Yi family — for the Chinese character for Yi is the same as that for plum. The surveys move to Han-yang.
summary.zh: 新朝既建，必遷新都。太祖初欲都雞龍山，工程已啟。然考得新羅時道詵禪師預言：『後世李氏當都漢陽。』高麗某王曾遍植梅樹於其地，且隨長隨伐，欲絕李氏之運——蓋朝鮮語李、梅同字。都遂定於漢陽。

sensitivity.note: Choson founding geomancy legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: According to unwritten law, with the beginning of a new dynasty a new capital must be founded, and King Tae-jo began to look about for a new site. At first he determined to build his capital at Kyeryong Mountain, and went so far as to begin work on it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: But it was found that in the days of Sil-la a celebrated priest, To-sun, had prophesied that in the days to come Yi would found a capital at Han-yang; and one of the Koryu kings had planted many plum trees at that place and as fast as they matured had them mutilated, hoping thus to harm the fortunes of the Yi family, for the Chinese character for Yi is the same as that for plum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Two commissioners were thereupon sent to Han-yang to make surveys for a palace site, and the capital of the new dynasty was planted there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Monk Muhak and the Two-Hundred-Year Warning

texts.period: Choson founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1394, fulfilled 1592

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Tradition says King Tae-jo had a dream in which a spirit told him that Kyeryong San was reserved for the capital of a future kingdom, so surveys moved to Han-yang. There the monk Mu-hak met the commissioners at Ha-yang and told them the palace should face toward Pagak Mountain and Mong-myuk Mountain; they persisted in facing it south. 'Very well,' the monk replied, 'if you do not listen to my advice you will have cause to remember it two hundred years from now.' His words were unheeded, but precisely two hundred years later, in 1592, the Japanese hordes of Hideyoshi landed on the shores of southern Korea.
summary.zh: 相傳太祖夢神人語曰：雞龍山乃留為他日之王都者，都遂遷漢陽。營宮室時，無學大師至，告使者曰：『宮當向爬開山、龍馬山。』使者不聽，定朝南。師曰：『不從吾言，二百年後必悔。』竟如其言，至萬曆二十年（1592）倭寇大舉登岸，是為報應之期。

sensitivity.note: Choson founding geomancy legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tradition also says that the king had a dream in which a spirit came and told him that Kyeryung San was reserved for the capital of a future kingdom which should be founded by a member of the Chong family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Two commissioners were thereupon sent to Han-yang to make surveys for a palace site. It is said that a monk, Mu-hak, met them at Ha-yang and told them that the palace should face toward Pagak Mountain and Mong-myuk Mountain, but they persisted in making it face the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Very well,' the monk replied, 'if you do not listen to my advice you will have cause to remember it two hundred years from now.' His words were unheeded, but precisely two hundred years later, in the year 1592, the Japanese hordes of Hideyoshi landed on the shores of southern Korea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

region.zh: 雞龍山，忠清道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Choson founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1392

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: King Tae-jo dreams that a spirit comes and tells him Kyeryong San is reserved for the capital of a future kingdom, to be founded by a member of the Chong family — a dream that redirects the dynasty from its first chosen site and leaves the mountain waiting for a Chong king who never came.
summary.zh: 太祖夜夢神人來告：雞龍山乃留與鄭氏子孫他日建都者。遂捨其地而都漢陽。山至今空留，以待未至之王。

sensitivity.note: Choson founding dream legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tradition says that the king had a dream in which a spirit came and told him that Kyeryung San was reserved for the capital of a future kingdom which should be founded by a member of the Chong family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Two commissioners were thereupon sent to Han-yang to make surveys for a palace site, and the site at Kyeryong was left to the future — a mountain kept waiting for a king of another name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hen that Swallowed the Silkworm

texts.period: Choson annal anecdote, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1398

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: An interesting prophecy is said to have been current at the time. The king dreamed that he saw a hen swallow a silkworm. No one could explain the dream until an official more imaginative than discreet averred that it meant Kyeryung would swallow Cham-du — kye means hen, and cham-du, silkworm's head, is the name of a spur of Nam-san. But Kyeryong was the site of the future capital of the next kingdom according to prophecy, so the interpretation was that the new dynasty would fall before another founded at Kyeryong. The poor fellow paid for this bright forecast with his life.
summary.zh: 相傳國初有讖。王夢見雞吞蠶，群臣莫解。有一臣強解曰：『雞吞蠶者，雞龍吞蠶頭也。』雞者雞龍，蠶頭乃南麓之山名。依舊讖雞龍乃後朝之都，是謂新朝將滅於雞龍之朝。此人以多言而遭誅。

sensitivity.note: Choson annal anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: An interesting prophecy is said to have been current at the time. The king dreamed that he saw a hen swallow a silk-worm. No one could explain the meaning of the dream until at last an official more imaginative than discreet averred that it meant that Kyeryung would swallow Cham-du. Kye means hen, and Cham-du, silkworm's head, is the name of one of the spurs of Nam-san in Seoul.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Kyeryong was the site of the future capital of the next kingdom according to prophecy, while silk-worm's head is the name of the spur; so the interpretation was that the new dynasty would fall before another founded at Kyeryong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The poor fellow paid for this bright forecast with his life.
